info:
Northern Europe lay beneath a vast ice sheet reaching almost 48°N, covering Scandinavia and most of Britain. Beyond its margin, annual temperatures were roughly 12°C colder than today, with winters dropping as much as 30°C colder.

Sea level stood some 120–125 metres below present, and the North Sea basin — later Doggerland — was largely dry, cold steppe.

The Baltic had not yet formed as a basin; meltwater was only beginning to pool at the ice margin, the earliest stage of what would become the Baltic Ice Lake. This was the coldest, driest configuration Europe would see during the Last Ice age.
background: Northern Europe lay under a vast ice sheet covering all of Scandinavia and most of Britain. Immediately south of the ice margin stretched a zone of polar desert — barren, wind-scoured periglacial terrain with virtually no vegetation cover, covering what is now the Netherlands, northern Germany, Belgium and southern Britain. Further south, the dominant landscape was open loess steppe and herb tundra: a cold, windswept plain dominated by grasses, Artemisia, Chenopodiaceae and a surprisingly rich forb layer including Thalictrum, Sanguisorba, Helianthemum and Armeria. This was not the uniform grass steppe it was once assumed to be — eDNA evidence shows forbs dominated over graminoids, pointing to large herbivores rather than fire as the main structuring force. Scattered microrefugia — sheltered valleys, south-facing slopes, possibly thermal springs — harboured isolated stands of Pinus and Betula. The southern fringe of the map, along the Atlantic coast of Iberia and in the foothills of the Pyrenees, Apennines and Balkans, supported open parkland and scattered deciduous woodland — the refugia from which postglacial recolonisation would later proceed. The North Sea basin (Doggerland) was largely exposed land, cold and dry, not yet the wetland it would become. Overall canopy cover across the map was minimal — perhaps 85–90% fully open, with open woodland only in southern refugial zones.
floraDescription:
The Last Glacial Maximum was characterised by the vast mammoth steppe, an open landscape of herb-rich grasslands, scattered shrubs and only isolated pockets of trees.

Contrary to traditional interpretations, this was not a barren polar desert but a remarkably diverse ecosystem filled with flowering plants, grasses and hardy shrubs. Large herds of mammoths, bison and wild horses continuously grazed, browsed and trampled the vegetation, preventing forests from becoming established despite local climatic conditions that could support scattered woodland.

Small refuges of pine and birch survived in sheltered valleys and southern regions, ready to recolonise Europe when the climate warmed.

Vegetation structure was shaped primarily by megaherbivores rather than by fire or human activity.
faunaDescription:
The Last Glacial Maximum was home to one of Europe's most remarkable ecosystems: the mammoth steppe.

Despite the cold climate, vast herb-rich grasslands stretched across much of northern Europe, maintained by enormous herds of grazing mammals like woolly mammoths, rhinoceroses, bison and wild horses. This rich herbivore community supported formidable predators such as cave lions and wolves.

Rivers, wetlands and scattered woodland refuges added further flora and fauna diversity to an otherwise open landscape.
